items.question: Per Sect. 7.1, what type of main rotor system and anti-torque design does the BK117 D-2 use?
options: Four-bladed hingeless main rotor with fibre-reinforced composite blades and a Fenestron anti-torque design
Two-bladed teetering main rotor with a conventional open tail rotor
Five-bladed bearingless main rotor with a Fenestron anti-torque design
Four-bladed articulated main rotor with a conventional open tail rotor
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1: the BK117 D-2 is a multi-purpose helicopter utilizing a four-bladed hingeless main rotor system with fibre-reinforced composite blades and a FENESTRON anti-torque design.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.1, on which side is the pilot's seat located?
options: The right-hand (RH) side
The left-hand (LH) side
Either side, per operator preference with no fixed default
Center console, tandem seating
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1: the pilot's seat is on the RH side of the BK117 D-2.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.1.1, through how many doors is the BK117 D-2 accessible in its standard configuration?
options: Six: two hinged crew doors, two sliding passenger doors, and two aft clam shell doors
Four: two hinged crew doors and two sliding passenger doors only
Eight, including two dedicated cargo hatches
Two: only the sliding passenger doors
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1.1: the BK117 D-2 is accessible through six doors — two hinged doors for the crew/front occupant, two sliding doors for the rear passengers, and two aft clam shell doors for the rear compartment.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.1.2, what components does the (detachable) tail boom consist of?
options: Horizontal stabilizer, vertical fin (including Fenestron structure), housing and gearbox
Only the vertical fin and horizontal stabilizer, with the Fenestron mounted on the fuselage
Tail rotor blades only, all other structure is part of the main fuselage
Horizontal stabilizer and main rotor mast extension
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1.2: the tail boom can be separated from the fuselage and consists of the horizontal stabilizer, vertical fin (including the Fenestron structure), housing, and gearbox.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.1, what is the approximate DC bus voltage when the electrical system is powered by the generators versus the main battery?
options: About 28V DC on generators, about 24V DC on battery power
About 24V DC on generators, about 28V DC on battery power
Both generators and battery supply exactly 24V DC at all times
Generators supply 115V AC; the battery supplies 28V DC
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.1: when operated by the generators, the system supplies about 28V DC to the airborne electrical system, and about 24V DC when operated by the battery; the standby battery supplies about 24V DC to emergency equipment.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.1, which busbar type connects the consumers of secondary importance that are shed in case of a double generator failure?
options: SHED BUSes 1 and 2
ESS BUSes 1 and 2
NON ESS BUSes 1 and 2
EMER BUS
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.1: SHED BUSes 1 and 2 connect consumers of secondary importance that are shed in case of a double generator failure; each is supplied by its MAIN BUS. ESS BUSes carry flight-essential consumers, NON ESS BUSes carry high-load consumers needing both generators/EPU, and the EMER BUS feeds IESI and emergency exit lights.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.1, which busbar directly supplies the standby air data and attitude indicator (IESI) and the emergency exit lights, with an alternate supply from the standby battery?
options: EMER BUS, supplied by ESS BUS 2
SHED BUS 1, supplied by MAIN BUS 1
NON ESS BUS 2, supplied by MAIN BUS 2
BAT BUS directly, with no ESS BUS involvement
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.1: the EMER BUS connects the standby air data and attitude indicator (IESI) and the emergency exit lights; it is supplied by ESS BUS 2, with an alternate power supply from the standby battery.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.2.1, how is a tripped generator reset and reconnected?
options: The GEN switch is momentarily set to the spring-loaded RES position, then released to return to NORM
The BAT MSTR switch must be cycled OFF and back ON
Only maintenance personnel can reset a generator on the ground
The BUS TIE switch for the opposite side must be turned OFF first
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.2.1: to reset and reconnect a generator, the GEN switch is momentarily set to the spring-loaded RES position and then released to return to the NORM position.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.3, what color is the generator state symbol when the generator is disconnected or degraded while its respective engine is still running?
options: Amber
Green
Light gray
Red
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.3: generator state symbol color logic — Green: connected; Amber: disconnected or degraded while its engine is running; Light gray: disconnected and its engine is off.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.3, what color is the battery state symbol used to indicate a battery overheat condition?
options: Red
Amber
Green
Light gray
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.3: battery state symbol color logic — Green: connected; Amber: disconnected or degraded; Red: battery overheat; Light gray: battery off, power provided by EPU.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.3, how is discharging vs. charging battery current represented in the digital indication?
options: Charging is shown as negative current, discharging as positive current
Charging is shown as positive current, discharging as negative current
Both are shown as positive values, distinguished only by color
Only discharging current is ever digitally displayed
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.3: battery charging is indicated as negative current, discharging as positive current; if the battery is discharged in flight, the battery current value is marked with an amber frame.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.4, when the optional GND PWR switch (not pushbutton variant) is activated, how long is ground power activation automatically limited to?
options: 10 minutes
45 minutes
60 minutes
Indefinitely, until manually switched off
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.4: for the GND PWR switch variant, activation is automatically limited to 10 minutes, after which power shuts off automatically (the GND PWR pushbutton variant is limited to 45 minutes instead).

items.question: Per Sect. 7.10.1, the bleed air heating system is automatically switched off by the FADEC under which condition?
options: As soon as engine power exceeds OEI maximum continuous (i.e. OEI 2 min or OEI 30 sec ratings are used)
Whenever the cabin temperature exceeds 25°C
Whenever both generators are online simultaneously
It is never automatically switched off by the FADEC; only the crew can switch it off
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.1: the bleed air heating system is automatically switched off by the FADEC as soon as engine power exceeds OEI maximum continuous (OEI 2 min or 30 sec ratings in use); it automatically returns to normal function once power reduces below OEI continuous.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.10.2, under what two conditions is the optional electrical heater active?
options: The bleed air heating system is on, AND demisting is selected (PUSH FOR DEFOG lever fully pushed)
The battery voltage exceeds 26V AND OAT is below 0°C
Both engines are at IDLE AND the aircraft is on the ground
The EPU is connected AND the avionics master switches are OFF
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.2: the electrical heater is active only when the bleed air heating system is on (heating symbol indicated) AND demisting is selected (PUSH FOR DEFOG lever fully pushed); it draws about 40A total (20A per generator).

items.question: Per Sect. 7.10.2, after switching off the electrical heater, for how long is it recommended to allow the ventilation to keep running?
options: At least 30 seconds
At least 5 minutes
At least 2 minutes
No cooldown period is recommended
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.2: it is recommended to allow the ventilation to run for at least 30 seconds after the electrical heater is switched off.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.10.3.1, what happens when the PUSH FOR AIR lever is pulled (rather than pushed)?
options: Air from the cockpit is recirculated, instead of outside air from the NACA inlet
Outside air from the NACA inlet is used for ventilation
The bleed air heating system is disabled entirely
It has no functional effect; it is a purely mechanical stow position
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.3.1: when the PUSH FOR AIR lever is pushed, outside air from the NACA inlet is used for ventilation; when pulled, air from the cockpit is recirculated instead.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.11.1.1, in which switch position does the emergency lighting system automatically activate on door opening, impact-switch activation, or ESS BUS 2 power loss?
options: ARM position
ON position
OFF position
It activates regardless of switch position
items.explanation: Sect. 7.11.1.1: with the INT LIGHTS EM/EX sw in the ARM position, emergency lighting switches on automatically in case of impact switch activation, an opened door, activation of the cabin EM/EXIT LT sw, or ESS BUS 2 power supply breakdown. The ON position turns all lights on unconditionally; OFF turns them all off.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.11.3.3, when must the (optional) cockpit dome light be switched off?
options: During flight
During ground operations only
Only when the EPU is disconnected
It has no restriction and may remain on at any time
items.explanation: Sect. 7.11.3.3 note: the cockpit dome light must be switched off during flight.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.11.5.2, which switch position on the collective grip controls the S/L (search and landing) light on the pilot side, and is it also controllable from the copilot's grip?
options: Controlled from the collective lever grip; equally controllable from the copilot's grip unless a second S/L light is installed
Controlled exclusively from the overhead panel, not from either collective grip
Only the copilot's collective grip can control the S/L light
The S/L light has no manual control; it activates automatically below 500 ft AGL
items.explanation: Sect. 7.11.5.2: the S/L lights are operated by switches on the pilot-side collective lever grip; unless a second S/L light is installed, the S/L light is equally controllable from the copilot's collective grip.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.1, how many axes does the AFCS control?
options: 4-axis
2-axis
3-axis
5-axis
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.1: the helicopter is equipped with a 4-axis AFCS, connected to the 28 V DC power system.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.4, what does a LEFT press of the cyclic stick's AP/BKUP ON switch do?
options: Simultaneously engages AP1 and sets back-up SAS in stand-by, and tries to recover a fully functional AP1 state by resetting transient failures
Simultaneously engages AP2 and sets back-up SAS in stand-by
Disengages AP1 and AP2 together, then arms back-up SAS
Engages tactical mode (TAC) only
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.4: a left press of AP/BKUP ON engages AP1 and sets back-up SAS in stand-by, attempting to recover a fully functional AP1 state by resetting transient failures. A right press does the equivalent for AP2.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.4, what does a double forward press of the AP/BKUP ON switch do in flight?
options: Provides quick engagement of the traditional upper modes (ALT, IAS, HDG/TRK) to establish a safe flight attitude, e.g. in case of disorientation
Engages tactical mode (TAC)
Disengages AFCS in two steps
Resets back-up SAS only, without engaging either autopilot
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.4: a double forward press of AP/BKUP ON in flight gives quick engagement of the traditional upper modes (ALT, IAS, HDG/TRK), establishing a safe flight attitude such as after disorientation. A long forward press instead engages tactical mode (TAC).

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.4, how does the AP/BKUP CUT switch disengage the AFCS?
options: In two steps: the first press disconnects AP1 and AP2, a re-press after 0.3 sec disconnects back-up SAS
In a single press that disconnects both autopilots and back-up SAS simultaneously
In three steps, disconnecting AP1, then AP2, then back-up SAS
It only disconnects back-up SAS; the autopilots must be disengaged separately on the APCP
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.4: AP/BKUP CUT disengages the AFCS in 2 steps - press once for AP1 and AP2 disconnection, then re-press after 0.3 sec to disconnect back-up SAS.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.4, what happens if the cyclic AP UM OFF button is pressed for more than 1 second while airborne?
options: It erases the pre-selected references of upper modes (e.g. ALT.A)
It approximately centers the cyclic stick and pedals
It engages the AFCS recovery function
It arms back-up SAS in stand-by
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.4: AP UM OFF disarms and disengages all upper modes. Pressed for more than 1 sec on the ground with the autopilot engaged, it centers the cyclic stick and pedals; pressed for more than 1 sec in flight, it instead erases pre-selected upper-mode references such as ALT.A.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.4, what does a double press of the cyclic GTC button do?
options: Engages HEIGHT and HOVER mode
Engages GTC mode only
Disengages all AFCS upper modes
Engages ALT.A mode
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.4: a single press of GTC engages GTC mode; a double press instead engages HEIGHT and HOVER mode.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.7, what happens if the AFCS recovery function is engaged while the helicopter is in a hover?
options: The aircraft will automatically accelerate to 40 KT
The aircraft remains in the hover and only wings-level attitude is captured
The recovery function is inhibited and cannot be engaged from a hover
The aircraft automatically climbs to a safe altitude before accelerating
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.7 CAUTION: when the AFCS recovery function (double forward press of AP/BKUP ON) is engaged from hover, the aircraft will automatically accelerate to 40 KT.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.7, what does back-up SAS provide and where is it implemented?
options: Stability augmentation on the pitch, roll, and yaw axes in case of loss of both autopilots, implemented in the stand-by instrument (IESI)
Full 4-axis autopilot function as a redundant backup to AP1/AP2, implemented in the APCP
Stability augmentation on the collective axis only, implemented in the trim actuator
A fully independent second AFCS computer with its own sensor suite
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.7: the back-up SAS mode provides stability augmentation on pitch, roll, and yaw axes in case of loss of both autopilots, and is implemented in the stand-by instrument (IESI).

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.9, what does a STEADY RED indication on an axis of the AFCS strip mean?
options: Total loss of stabilization on the affected axis, requiring hands-on piloting
Minor degradation causing the system to be fail-passive instead of fail-operative
The upper mode is armed and functioning normally
Pilot override action is in progress
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.9: on the AFCS strip, RED steady means total loss of stabilization on the affected axis, requiring hands-on piloting; RED inverse video flashing means manual recovery or the pilot's immediate attention is required.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.9, on the AFCS strip, what does a CYAN inverse-video-flashing indication mean, and what should the pilot do?
options: The upper mode is about to disarm automatically; the pilot shall re-arm it if required
The upper mode has already disarmed; no pilot action is possible
The axis has totally lost stabilization; the pilot must take manual control
The mode is engaged and functioning normally; no action is needed
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.9: CYAN inverse video flashing on the AFCS strip means an armed upper mode is about to disarm automatically, and the pilot shall re-arm it if required. CYAN steady instead means the upper mode is armed (normal operation).

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.10, on the AFCS status area, what does a GREY component color indicate?
options: Inactive - either failed but recoverable via the AP/BKUP ON switch on the cyclic, or deliberately deactivated by the pilot
Failed and unrecoverable
Active, but on stand-by
Degraded but still functioning
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.10: GREY on the AFCS status area means the component is inactive - either it failed but the failure can be recovered via the AP/BKUP ON switch on the cyclic, or it was deliberately deactivated by the pilot. RED means failed (unrecoverable), CYAN means active but stand-by, and AMBER means degraded.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.12, when coupling the autopilot to a navigation source via the MFD, what does it mean if the coupling key shows no label at all?
options: Coupling is inactive
The autopilot is coupled to the selected navigation source
The autopilot is armed but not yet coupled
A navigation source fault is present
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.12: the coupling key label is CPL (couples to the selected source), DCPL (decouples), or DISARM (disarms the autopilot) - or it disappears entirely, which means coupling is inactive.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.2, what is the difference between the HDG+VS and TRK+FPA mode combinations selected on the APCP's HDG-VS/TRK-FPA switch?
options: HDG+VS is the traditional combination, while TRK+FPA is GPS-based
HDG+VS is only available in IFR, while TRK+FPA is VFR-only
TRK+FPA is the traditional combination, while HDG+VS is GPS-based
There is no functional difference; the switch only changes the display format
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.2: the HDG-VS/TRK-FPA rotary switch on the APCP selects between mode combinations HDG+VS (traditional) or TRK+FPA (GPS based).

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.5, why does the back-up SAS function use only one SEMA actuator set (SEMA set No. 1) in the pitch, roll, and yaw axes?
options: For safety reasons
Because SEMA set No. 2 is reserved exclusively for the collective axis
Because SEMA set No. 2 only operates when both autopilots are engaged
Because SEMA set No. 1 has greater control authority than SEMA set No. 2
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.5: pitch, roll, and yaw each have two SEMA actuators, but for safety reasons the back-up SAS function uses only one SEMA actuator (SEMA set No. 1) per axis.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (ALT MODE), what is the minimum ground height required to engage ALT mode?
options: 30 ft
50 ft
100 ft
0 ft (no minimum)
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 ALT MODE Conditions & Limitations: the minimum altitude (ground height) to engage ALT mode is 30 ft.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (ALT MODE), what happens automatically when ground proximity is detected during a descent on any vertical upper mode (except CRHT)?
options: The AFCS automatically reverts to ALT mode
The AFCS automatically disengages completely
The AFCS automatically engages CRHT mode
Nothing; the pilot must intervene manually
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 ALT MODE, Automatic engagement: the AFCS automatically reverts from any vertical upper mode (except CRHT) to ALT mode when ground proximity is detected in descent.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (IAS MODE), what happens automatically if airspeed drops below the 60 kt protection speed while a vertical mode (e.g. ALT, VS) is engaged on the pitch axis?
options: The vertical mode is transferred to the collective axis and IAS mode is engaged on the pitch axis
The AFCS disengages the vertical mode entirely
The vertical mode remains on the pitch axis and IAS mode is inhibited
The aircraft automatically enters a hover
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 IAS MODE, Automatic engagement: if airspeed drops below the 60 kt protection speed while a vertical mode is engaged on the pitch axis, and the collective axis is available, the vertical mode transfers to the collective axis and IAS mode engages on the pitch axis.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (VS MODE), what happens automatically as the helicopter approaches the ground with VS mode engaged?
options: VS mode automatically changes to ALT mode to achieve a level off at 150 ft
VS mode automatically changes to CRHT mode
VS mode disengages with no automatic level-off
The vertical speed reference is automatically set to zero at 500 ft
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 VS MODE, Automatic level off: when approaching the ground, VS mode is automatically changed to ALT mode, to achieve a level off at 150 ft.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (ALT.A MODE), if an ALT.A reference is preselected but ALT.A mode is not engaged, when does the "ALT.A crossing" voice message sound?
options: Only on the first crossing of the reference; it will not sound again on subsequent crossings
Every time the aircraft crosses the reference altitude
Only after the reference has been crossed three times
It never sounds unless ALT.A mode is engaged
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 ALT.A MODE: the "ALT.A crossing" voice message will sound only on the first crossing of a preselected but unengaged ALT.A reference; on subsequent crossings it will not sound.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (CRHT MODE with FLY-UP), when is the FLY-UP protection mode automatically engaged, and what does it command?
options: When the aircraft descends below 200 ft, or 30 ft below the CRHT reference (whichever is lower); it commands maximum climb rate and sounds "AUTOPILOT FLYUP"
When the aircraft climbs above the CRHT reference by more than 30 ft; it commands a descent
Only when the radar altimeter signal is lost; it disengages CRHT mode entirely
When airspeed exceeds 60 kt while CRHT is engaged; it commands a speed reduction
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 CRHT MODE with FLY-UP: FLY-UP is automatically engaged when the aircraft descends below whichever is lower of 200 ft or 30 ft below the CRHT reference. It commands maximum climb rate, the AFCS strip shows FLYUP flashing, and the voice message "AUTOPILOT FLYUP" sounds.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (LOC MODE) CAUTION, what can happen if the final approach course is set incorrectly before engaging LOC mode?
options: Erratic course changes or roll oscillations may occur
The LOC mode will simply refuse to arm
The autopilot will automatically correct the course setting
GS mode will compensate for the error
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 LOC MODE CAUTION: for the autopilot to function properly, the final course must be set correctly. If the course is set incorrectly, erratic course changes or roll oscillations may occur.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13, if the navigation signal is lost while a mode is armed, after how many seconds does the "AP DISARM" voice message sound for LOC mode versus VOR mode?
options: 10 sec for LOC, 30 sec for VOR
30 sec for LOC, 10 sec for VOR
10 sec for both LOC and VOR
30 sec for both LOC and VOR
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13: for LOC mode, "AP DISARM" sounds 10 sec after the armed mode's signal is lost or the frequency is changed; for VOR mode, the same voice message sounds after 30 sec.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (GS MODE), if the glide slope signal is lost while GS mode is armed and then becomes available again, what happens?
options: GS mode automatically re-arms, as long as LOC mode is not disarmed/decoupled
GS mode stays disarmed and must be re-armed manually via the MFD
GS mode automatically engages immediately without re-arming
LOC mode is also automatically disarmed
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 GS MODE: if the GS signal is lost while armed and becomes available again, GS mode will automatically re-arm, as long as the LOC mode is not disarmed/decoupled.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (V.APP MODE), at what height above the ground does V.APP automatically revert to ALT mode to level off, and does it depend on the Level of Service used?
options: Yes - 65 ft above ground for LPV, 150 ft above ground for LNAV/VNAV
No - always 150 ft above ground regardless of Level of Service
No - always 65 ft above ground regardless of Level of Service
Yes - 150 ft for LPV, 65 ft for LNAV/VNAV
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 V.APP MODE, Automatic level off: V.APP automatically reverts to ALT mode to level the aircraft off at 65 ft above the ground when LPV Level of Service is used, or 150 ft above the ground if LNAV/VNAV Level of Service is used.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (V.APP MODE), how is the airspeed reference managed prior to the FAF during a V.APP-coupled approach?
options: It is automatically set so that the rate of descent does not exceed 1000 ft/min
It is fixed at VY regardless of descent rate
The pilot must manually adjust IAS to control descent rate
It is automatically reduced to the minimum airspeed for the aircraft configuration
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 V.APP MODE, Airspeed management: prior to the FAF, the IAS reference is automatically set so that the rate of descent during the approach does not exceed 1000 ft/min.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (VOR MODE), what does the AFCS do while the aircraft crosses the "cone of silence" directly over a VOR station?
options: It maintains the current heading, then resumes tracking once the aircraft exits the cone of silence
It automatically disarms VOR mode and reverts to ATT mode
It commands an immediate turn to intercept the outbound radial
It ignores the bearing signal variations and continues tracking the previous radial unchanged
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 VOR MODE: while crossing the cone of silence over the VOR station, the bearing signal shows fast, large-amplitude variations and becomes invalid for some time. The mode maintains the current heading, and tracking resumes when exiting the cone of silence.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (NAV MODE), how does the maximum bank angle used for track changes evolve during a turn?
options: Standard rate turns (max. 21° bank) for the first 60 sec, then up to 30° bank is allowed afterward
A constant maximum of 30° bank throughout the entire turn
A constant maximum of 21° bank throughout the entire turn
45° bank for the first 60 sec, then reduced to 21° bank
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 NAV MODE: track changes are conducted with standard rate turns (max. 21° bank) for the first 60 sec; after 60 sec, a maximum of 30° bank angle is allowed, depending on the FMS command.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13, the GTC, HOVER, and Helicopter TAKEOFF modes all carry the same CAUTION. What does it say?
options: These modes rely on GPS and magnetic heading, and shall not be used with poor GPS reception or magnetic heading perturbations - the DG mode with correct heading shall be used instead
These modes are inhibited below 500 ft AGL and shall not be used at low altitude
These modes require both autopilots to be engaged and shall not be used with only one AP active
These modes are for VFR use only and shall not be used in IMC
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13: GTC, HOVER, and Helicopter TAKEOFF mode all carry the same CAUTION - they rely on GPS and magnetic heading. In case of poor GPS reception (e.g. in a canyon, or with an associated GTN message) they shall not be used; in case of magnetic heading perturbations (e.g. near large metallic structures, or MAG DEGR indicated) the DG mode with correct heading shall be used instead.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (HOVER MODE), what happens automatically in the vertical axis when HOVER mode is engaged?
options: HEIGHT mode is automatically engaged in the vertical axis
CRHT mode is automatically engaged in the vertical axis
The vertical axis is left uncontrolled; the pilot must fly the collective manually
ALT mode is automatically engaged in the vertical axis
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 HOVER MODE: with engagement of HOVER mode, the HEIGHT mode is automatically engaged in the vertical axis.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (HELICOPTER TAKEOFF MODE), if an engine failure occurs during the climb in REARWARD TAKEOFF or VERTICAL TAKEOFF, versus during the GO AROUND phase, what happens automatically in each case?
options: During the climb: the REJECTED submode engages automatically to bring the helicopter back to the helipad (cushioning/touchdown flown manually). During GO AROUND: the CONTINUED TAKEOFF submode engages automatically to accelerate to at least VTOSS with a 1000 ft/min climb
In both cases the AFCS disengages completely and the pilot must fly manually
During the climb: CONTINUED TAKEOFF engages. During GO AROUND: REJECTED engages
The Helicopter TAKEOFF mode has no automatic response to engine failure in either phase
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 HELICOPTER TAKEOFF MODE, Automatic engagement: if an engine failure occurs during the climb in REARWARD TAKEOFF or VERTICAL TAKEOFF, the REJECTED submode engages automatically to bring the helicopter back towards the helipad, with cushioning and final touchdown flown manually. If the failure occurs during the GO AROUND phase, the CONTINUED TAKEOFF submode engages automatically to accelerate to at least VTOSS with a 1000 ft/min rate of climb.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (TAC MODE), under what conditions is use of the tactical (TAC) mode permitted?
options: Only in VFR conditions with good visual references, flown manually or attentive hands-on
In IMC only, as a substitute for a coupled approach
In any conditions, since TAC mode provides full hands-off stabilization
Only during Cat A takeoff and landing procedures
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 TAC MODE, Conditions & Limitations: use of the TAC mode is permitted only in VFR conditions with good visual references, and the mode shall be flown manually or attentive hands-on.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.13 (GA MODE), for how long does GA mode remain active before transferring control to VS/FPA and IAS mode, and how does this differ between cruise and hover?
options: Typically 15 sec in cruise and 30 sec from hover
Typically 30 sec in cruise and 15 sec from hover
A fixed 20 sec regardless of the flight condition at engagement
GA mode remains active indefinitely until manually disengaged
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.13 GA MODE, Conditions & Limitations: GA mode is active for a few seconds - typically 15 sec in cruise and 30 sec from hover - and then transfers control to the VS/FPA mode and IAS mode.
